listeningParts.title: Booking a venue for a research conference
listeningParts.contextDescription: A conference organiser phones a hotel events manager to book facilities for an academic conference.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Good morning, Kingsway Hotel events team, this is Martin.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Hello, Martin. My name is Dr Helen Kowalczyk, and I'm organising a two-day psychology conference in the autumn. I spoke to one of your colleagues last week, and she suggested I call you to discuss the details.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Of course, Dr Kowalczyk. Could I just take the spelling of your surname?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Certainly. It's K-O-W-A-L-C-Z-Y-K.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Thank you. So, how many delegates are you expecting?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: We originally planned for about two hundred, but registrations have been much higher than expected, so we're now looking at around two hundred and eighty.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: That's fine. Our main conference room, the Regency Suite, holds up to three hundred and fifty in theatre style, so you'd have plenty of space for your plenary sessions. What dates were you considering?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: The fourteenth and fifteenth of October, which is a Thursday and Friday.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Let me check. Yes, the Regency Suite is available on both days. Will you need smaller rooms for parallel sessions?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, we'll have four parallel sessions running at the same time in the afternoons, so we'd need four breakout rooms, each seating about sixty to seventy people.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We have five rooms of that size on the first floor, so that's no problem. They all have projectors and screens. Will your speakers need anything else in the way of equipment?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Microphones in every room, please, because some of our speakers have quite quiet voices. And in the main suite, we'd like the plenary talks to be recorded and streamed online for members who can't attend in person.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We can do that, but streaming requires one of our technicians to be present throughout, which is an additional charge of three hundred and fifty pounds per day.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's acceptable. Now, catering. We'd like tea and coffee on arrival and twice during the day, and a buffet lunch.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Our standard day delegate package covers exactly that: room hire, refreshments and a hot buffet lunch, at fifty-two pounds per person per day. For groups over two hundred and fifty, we can reduce that to forty-eight.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's helpful. About fifteen per cent of our delegates have dietary requirements, mostly vegetarian, but some vegan and a few gluten-free. Is that manageable?

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: Absolutely. We'll just need a final list two weeks before the event. Are you planning a conference dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Yes, on the Thursday evening. We expect about a hundred and fifty people.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: The dinner would be in the Garden Restaurant, which overlooks the river. It seats up to a hundred and eighty, so that works well. A three-course dinner is sixty-five pounds per person, including a glass of wine.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And accommodation? Many delegates will travel from abroad.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We can hold a block of rooms at a discounted conference rate. I'd suggest eighty rooms initially. Delegates book directly using a special code, and any rooms not booked six weeks before the conference are released back to us, so you're not charged for them.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: That's ideal, because we can't predict exactly how many will stay. What about getting here? Some of our delegates won't be familiar with the city.

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: We're about ten minutes' walk from the central railway station. If you'd like, we can provide a shuttle bus from the airport on the Wednesday evening and Thursday morning, but that needs to be booked at least a month in advance.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Let's do that. And what do you need from me to confirm the booking?

dialogue.speaker: Events manager
dialogue.text: I'll email you a contract. We ask for a deposit of twenty-five per cent when you sign, and the balance thirty days after the event. If you need to reduce numbers, you can do so without penalty up to fourteen days beforehand.

dialogue.speaker: Organiser
dialogue.text: Perfect. I'll look out for your email.

listeningParts.title: Inside a memory research laboratory
listeningParts.contextDescription: A research coordinator welcomes volunteers who have signed up to take part in memory experiments.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone, and thank you for volunteering to take part in our research. My name is Dr Amara Osei, and I coordinate the participant programme here at the Centre for Memory Research. Before we start, I'd like to explain what we do, what taking part involves, and your rights as participants.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The Centre was established twelve years ago, and our research focuses on how memories are formed, stored and retrieved, and why they sometimes go wrong. One of our main projects at the moment looks at how sleep affects memory. Another investigates false memories: how people can come to remember, quite sincerely, events that never actually happened. And a third project, funded by a national charity, is studying early changes in memory that might help doctors detect dementia sooner.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: You've all been placed in one of three groups, depending on which studies you're eligible for. The largest group will take part in computer-based tasks in our testing rooms on the ground floor. These usually involve learning lists of words or pictures and then being tested on them later. A typical session lasts about an hour, and you'll be paid fifteen dollars for each session.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The second group will take part in our sleep study. This involves spending two nights in our sleep laboratory, which is on the third floor. You'll learn some material in the evening, sleep with sensors attached to your head to monitor your brain activity, and be tested the following morning. Because it's a bigger commitment, participants in this study receive two hundred dollars in total.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: The third and smallest group will have a brain scan. The scanner is in the hospital next door, and you'll be taken there by one of our researchers. Scans are completely safe and painless, but they can be noisy, and you need to lie very still inside a narrow tube for about forty-five minutes. If you think you might feel uncomfortable in enclosed spaces, please tell us now, and we can move you to a different study with no problem at all.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Now, a few important points about your rights. Before you take part in any study, you'll be asked to read an information sheet and sign a consent form. Please read these carefully and ask questions if anything is unclear. Taking part is entirely voluntary, and you can withdraw from any study at any time without giving a reason. If you withdraw, you'll still be paid for the time you've already spent with us.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: All the information we collect is kept confidential. Your results are stored under a code number rather than your name, and they're anonymised before being published, so nobody will be able to identify you. Your personal details are stored separately and are deleted five years after the study ends.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Some of our studies involve a small amount of deception. For instance, in some memory experiments, we can't tell you in advance that you'll be tested later, because knowing that would change how you pay attention. But at the end of every study, a researcher will explain exactly what the study was about and why any information was withheld. This is called debriefing, and you can ask as many questions as you like.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: A couple of practical things. Please arrive ten minutes before your session, and if you can't make it, let us know at least twenty-four hours in advance so we can offer the slot to someone else. Payments are made by bank transfer within two weeks. And if you're interested in the results, you can sign up for our newsletter, which summarises our findings in plain language a few times a year.

dialogue.speaker: Coordinator
dialogue.text: Finally, please don't discuss the details of the experiments with friends who might take part later, as that could affect the results. Right, my colleagues will now take each group to complete the paperwork.

listeningParts.title: Discussing the replication crisis
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two psychology students, Felix and Nora, discuss the "replication crisis" with their tutor in preparation for an essay.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: So, your essay question is about the replication crisis in psychology. Felix, can you start by explaining what the term refers to?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: Sure. Basically, replication means repeating a study to see if you get the same result. Around 2015, a large project tried to repeat a hundred studies published in leading psychology journals, and only about a third to a half of them produced results that were statistically significant the second time. That led people to talk about a crisis, because it suggested that many published findings might not be reliable.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. And Nora, what are the main explanations for why so many studies failed to replicate?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: There are several. One is small samples. If you only test twenty or thirty people, a result can easily appear by chance. Another is what's called publication bias: journals were much more likely to publish studies with positive, exciting results than ones that found nothing, so the published literature gave a misleading picture.

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: And then there are questionable research practices. Not fraud exactly, but things like collecting more data until the result becomes significant, or testing lots of different measures and only reporting the ones that worked. Each decision might seem reasonable, but together they greatly increase the chance of a false positive.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, one thing I'd warn you about in the essay is suggesting that psychology is uniquely bad. What would you say to that?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: That similar problems have been found in other fields. There was a project in cancer biology that had trouble replicating important studies, and economics has had similar debates. Psychology may just have been more open about investigating the problem.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: I'd agree. In some ways, psychology has led the response. What reforms have been introduced?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: The one I find most convincing is pre-registration. Researchers publish their hypotheses and their planned analysis before they collect any data. That way, they can't change their predictions after seeing the results.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: And there are now journals that offer what are called registered reports, where the journal agrees to publish a study based on its design, before the results are known. That removes the incentive to produce exciting findings.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Are there any drawbacks to pre-registration?

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: Some researchers say it makes it harder to do exploratory research, where you don't know in advance what you'll find. But I think that's a misunderstanding. You can still explore; you just have to be clear about which results were predicted and which were discovered afterwards.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I'm a bit more sceptical than Felix. Pre-registration helps, but it depends on people actually following their plans. I read a study that found a lot of pre-registered papers didn't stick to what they'd registered, and nobody noticed.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a good point to include, and it shows critical thinking. What about the famous findings that didn't replicate? Did you choose an example?

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: We were thinking of power posing, the idea that standing in a confident posture for two minutes changes your hormone levels and makes you take more risks. It became hugely popular after a talk was watched millions of times online, but larger studies didn't find the hormone effects.

dialogue.speaker: Felix
dialogue.text: Although some studies still find that people report feeling slightly more confident. So it's not that the whole idea was wrong, just that the original claims were too strong.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That nuance is exactly what I'd like to see. Be careful not to suggest the original researchers were dishonest; there's no evidence of that. For the conclusion, I'd encourage you to argue whether the crisis has ultimately been good for the discipline.

dialogue.speaker: Nora
dialogue.text: I think we both agree it has, in the long run.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Then make that case, but acknowledge that it's damaged public trust in the short term. Send me a plan by Wednesday.

listeningParts.title: How we make decisions
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a psychology course on heuristics and biases in human decision-making.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. Today we turn to one of the most influential areas of modern psychology: the study of how people make decisions under uncertainty, and why those decisions so often depart from what we might consider rational. Much of this work began with two Israeli psychologists, Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, whose research in the 1970s challenged the assumption, common in economics, that people generally make logical choices that maximise their own interests.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Kahneman later described the mind as using two different systems of thinking. System One is fast, automatic and intuitive; it's what allows you to recognise a friend's face instantly or to understand a simple sentence without effort. System Two is slow, deliberate and effortful; it's what you use to solve a difficult mathematical problem or fill in a tax form. Most of the time, System One works extremely well. But it relies on mental shortcuts, known as heuristics, which can lead to systematic errors, or biases.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Let me give you three examples. The first is the availability heuristic: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind. Events that are dramatic or widely reported, such as plane crashes or shark attacks, are easy to recall, so people tend to overestimate their frequency. Meanwhile, far more common causes of death, such as heart disease, receive less attention and are underestimated. After a major accident is reported in the news, for example, sales of insurance against that kind of accident often rise sharply, even though the actual risk hasn't changed.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The second is anchoring. In one famous experiment, Tversky and Kahneman spun a wheel of fortune that had been fixed to stop at either ten or sixty-five. Participants were then asked to estimate the percentage of African countries in the United Nations. Those who had seen the number sixty-five gave much higher estimates than those who had seen ten, even though the number on the wheel was obviously random. Anchoring effects have since been found among experienced professionals, including judges deciding on sentences and estate agents valuing houses.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The third example is framing. People's choices can be influenced by how options are described, even when the underlying facts are identical. In one well-known study, participants were told that a disease was expected to kill six hundred people and asked to choose between two programmes. When the options were described in terms of lives saved, most people chose the certain option. When exactly the same options were described in terms of deaths, most people chose the risky option. This finding has obvious implications for how doctors present information about treatments to patients.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Underlying many of these patterns is a principle Kahneman and Tversky called loss aversion: losses feel roughly twice as painful as equivalent gains feel pleasurable. This helps to explain why people often hold on to investments that are falling in value, hoping to avoid realising a loss, and why they may refuse a bet with a fifty per cent chance of winning a hundred and fifty pounds and a fifty per cent chance of losing a hundred, even though, on average, they would gain.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Now, it would be wrong to conclude from this research that humans are simply irrational. Some psychologists, notably Gerd Gigerenzer, have argued that heuristics are often remarkably effective, especially in real-world environments where information is limited and time is short. A simple rule of thumb may outperform complex calculations when the future is genuinely uncertain. The question, then, is not whether heuristics are good or bad, but in which environments they serve us well.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: This research has had a major practical impact. Kahneman was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2002, an unusual honour for a psychologist. Tversky had died in 1996, and the prize is not awarded after death. Their ideas have since influenced fields as diverse as medicine, law, finance and public policy, and we'll look at some of these applications next week.

readingPassages.title: The man who could not forget
paragraphs: In the 1920s, a young Russian journalist named Solomon Shereshevsky was sent by his editor to see the psychologist Alexander Luria. The editor had noticed that Shereshevsky never took notes at the daily morning meeting, yet could repeat every instruction word for word. Shereshevsky himself saw nothing remarkable in this; he assumed that everyone remembered in the same way. Luria began testing him, expecting to find the limits of his memory quickly, as he would with any other subject. Instead, over a period of some thirty years, he found that there appeared to be no limit at all.

Luria presented Shereshevsky with long lists of words, numbers and nonsense syllables, and found that he could recall them perfectly, forwards or backwards, after hearing them once. More astonishingly, he could reproduce the same lists when tested again months or even, on some occasions, more than a decade later, without having been warned that he would be tested. In the book he eventually wrote about the case, Luria described his subject's memory as having, for practical purposes, no measurable capacity and no measurable decline over time.

Part of the explanation seemed to lie in an unusual condition called synaesthesia, in which stimulation of one sense automatically produces sensations in another. For Shereshevsky, sounds and words triggered vivid images, colours, tastes and even textures. A particular tone might appear to him as a strip of reddish-orange light, and he once told the psychologist Lev Vygotsky that he had 'such a crumbly, yellow voice'. These rich associations made each item to be remembered highly distinctive, and therefore easy to recall. Numbers, too, took on personalities for him: the number one was a proud, well-built man, while seven was a man with a moustache. Such vivid, almost cinematic associations are rare even among people with synaesthesia, and they appear to have been central to his abilities.

Shereshevsky also used deliberate techniques. When memorising a list, he would imagine walking along a familiar street, such as Gorky Street in Moscow, and place an image of each item at a particular point along the route, outside a house, beside a fence or in a shop window. To recall the list, he simply walked along the street again in his imagination and 'saw' the objects. This technique, known as the method of loci, has been used since ancient times; Greek and Roman orators used it to memorise long speeches. Interestingly, Shereshevsky's rare errors usually occurred not because he had forgotten an item but because he had placed it somewhere poorly lit, or against a background of the same colour, so that he failed to 'see' it.

His extraordinary memory, however, was far from an unqualified advantage. Shereshevsky found it very difficult to forget, and his mind was often crowded with images from the past that he could not suppress. He struggled with abstract ideas and with metaphors, because every word called up a concrete image that interfered with the meaning. Poetry was particularly hard for him. He also had trouble recognising faces, because a person's face changed constantly with their expression and the light, so that each version seemed like a separate image. After leaving journalism, he tried several jobs before eventually earning his living as a professional memory performer, giving demonstrations on stage.

Modern researchers have studied a small number of people with a condition now called highly superior autobiographical memory, who can remember what happened on almost every day of their lives, often including the weather and what they ate. Unlike Shereshevsky, however, these individuals are generally no better than average at memorising lists of words or numbers. Their remarkable recall is limited to events from their own lives, and some researchers believe it may be linked to a tendency to rehearse personal memories obsessively.

Such cases are fascinating partly because they challenge our assumption that a better memory would always be desirable. Many psychologists now argue that forgetting is not simply a failure of memory but an essential part of how it works. By allowing unimportant details to fade, forgetting helps us to generalise from experience, to focus on what matters and to adapt when circumstances change. Shereshevsky's life suggests that a mind that retains everything may find it harder, not easier, to understand the world.

readingPassages.title: The science of habits
paragraphs: Much of what we do each day is not the result of conscious decision. Researchers who asked people to record their actions at regular intervals found that roughly forty per cent of everyday behaviour was performed almost every day, usually in the same place, and often while the person was thinking about something else. Brushing our teeth, checking our phones, taking a particular route to work: these actions are governed less by intention than by habit. Understanding how habits form, and how they can be changed, has therefore become a major concern for psychologists, doctors and public health officials.

A habit, in the psychological sense, is an action that is triggered automatically by a cue in the environment as a result of repeated association. The cue might be a place, a time of day, an emotional state or the presence of particular people. Each time the action is performed in response to the cue and followed by a reward, the link between them becomes stronger. Eventually, the cue alone is enough to prompt the behaviour, even when the reward is no longer valued. In one experiment, people who habitually ate popcorn at the cinema ate just as much stale, week-old popcorn as fresh popcorn, provided they were in a cinema; in a meeting room, by contrast, they ate far less of the stale variety.

Neuroscientists have traced the shift from deliberate action to habit to changes in the brain. When we first learn a behaviour, areas involved in planning and decision-making are highly active. As the behaviour is repeated, control gradually passes to a group of structures deep in the brain known as the basal ganglia, which allows the action to be carried out with little conscious effort. This frees mental resources for other tasks, which is why habits are so useful: imagine having to think carefully about every movement involved in driving or typing.

How long does it take to form a habit? A popular claim, repeated in countless self-help books, is that it takes twenty-one days. This figure appears to come from a 1960s book by a plastic surgeon, who observed that patients took about three weeks to get used to changes in their appearance, and it has no basis in research on habits. In a study published in 2009, participants chose a new healthy behaviour, such as drinking a glass of water after breakfast or going for a run before dinner, and reported daily how automatic it felt. The average time to reach maximum automaticity was sixty-six days, but there was enormous variation, from eighteen days to an estimated two hundred and fifty-four. Simpler behaviours became automatic more quickly, and missing a single day did not significantly affect the process.

One implication of habit research is that good intentions are often not enough. People who intend to eat more healthily or exercise more regularly frequently fail, not because they lack willpower, but because their environment continues to trigger old habits. Research suggests that a more effective strategy is to change the environment itself, so that the cues for unwanted habits are removed and cues for desired ones are added. Keeping fruit on the kitchen table rather than biscuits, or placing running shoes by the door, may achieve more than determination alone.

Major life changes offer a particular opportunity. When people move house, start a new job or have a child, the familiar cues that maintained their habits are disrupted, and behaviour becomes more open to deliberate choice. Researchers have described this as the 'habit discontinuity hypothesis'. In one study, people who had recently moved home were more likely to change their method of travel to work after receiving information about environmentally friendly options than people who had lived in the same place for longer. Some public health campaigns now deliberately target people at such moments.

Another useful technique is what psychologists call implementation intentions: specific plans that link a behaviour to a particular situation, in the form 'When situation X arises, I will do Y.' For example, rather than simply intending to floss their teeth more often, a person might decide, 'After I brush my teeth at night, I will floss.' Dozens of studies have found that forming such plans substantially increases the chances that people will follow through on their intentions, apparently because they create a new cue-action link that the person can rely on without needing to remember or decide.

readingPassages.title: Is free will an illusion?
paragraphs: In 1983, the American neuroscientist Benjamin Libet published the results of an experiment that has been debated ever since. Participants were asked to flex their wrist whenever they felt the urge to do so, while watching a special clock and noting the position of a moving dot at the moment they first became aware of the decision to move. At the same time, electrodes on their scalp recorded a pattern of brain activity known as the readiness potential, which was already known to precede voluntary movements. Libet found that the readiness potential began, on average, about a third of a second before participants reported being aware of their decision.

To many commentators, the implication seemed obvious and startling. If the brain begins preparing an action before we are conscious of deciding to act, then our sense of consciously choosing may be an illusion; the real decision, on this view, is made by unconscious brain processes, and conscious awareness merely follows. Later experiments using brain scanning appeared to strengthen this conclusion. In one study, researchers were able to predict, with an accuracy somewhat better than chance, which of two buttons a participant would press up to several seconds before the participant reported making the decision.

Libet himself did not draw such a radical conclusion. He noted that there remained a brief window, around a fifth of a second, between conscious awareness and the movement itself, during which participants could still veto the action. Free will, he suggested, might operate not by initiating actions but by allowing or blocking them, a capacity sometimes described as 'free won't'. Critics have pointed out, though, that if the decision to veto is itself caused by earlier brain activity, this merely moves the problem back a step.

More recent research has challenged the interpretation of the readiness potential itself. In 2012, a team led by Aaron Schurger proposed that the gradual build-up of activity reflects not a decision being made unconsciously, but the random fluctuations of neural activity that occur all the time. In a task where people are asked to move at an arbitrary moment for no reason, they argued, the movement is likely to occur when these fluctuations happen to cross a threshold. Averaged across many trials, this produces a curve that looks like a slow preparation for action, even though no decision was being made in advance. If this is correct, the readiness potential tells us little about when decisions are actually made.

There are also doubts about whether the experiments study the kind of decision that matters. Flexing a wrist at a random moment is a choice with no reasons and no consequences. Most decisions that we care about, such as accepting a job or ending a relationship, involve weighing reasons over hours, days or even months. A study by Uri Maoz and colleagues found that the readiness potential was present when participants made arbitrary choices between two charities, but largely absent when the choice was meaningful because the selected charity would actually receive a donation. It seems unwise, I would suggest, to draw sweeping conclusions about human freedom from laboratory tasks that are so unlike the choices of real life.

Philosophers, meanwhile, point out that the experiments may not address the real question at all. Many philosophers are what is called compatibilists: they argue that free will is compatible with the idea that all events, including our decisions, have prior causes. On this view, an action is free not because it is uncaused, but because it flows from the person's own desires, values and reasoning, rather than from external force or compulsion. Unconscious brain processes are, after all, still processes within the person. For a compatibilist, discovering that decisions begin in neural activity before conscious awareness is no more threatening to freedom than discovering that thoughts are made of neurons.

Does any of this matter outside the laboratory? Some research suggests it might. In one study, participants who read a passage arguing that free will is an illusion subsequently behaved less honestly in a test where cheating was possible than those who read a neutral passage. Although attempts to repeat this finding have produced mixed results, it raises the possibility that how we think about free will may influence how we behave. My own view is that the neuroscience has added valuable detail to our understanding of how actions are produced, but that it has not, so far, settled one of philosophy's oldest questions.
